name: Marco Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead a crew repairing electricity lines along the harbour roads. My two-year technical diploma and years on those old feeders help me spot a bad switch label before anybody climbs. I still like seeing a row of houses light up; the cold bucket shifts make my joints complain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cooks at a school, and our grown children live on their own. My line pay is typical for the job, we have around four months of expenses saved and there are some other utilities nearby. Retirement is in sight but we have not set a date, and I have never used an AI tool; I take safety and apprentice questions to our union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office can have its quicker forms, but a lineworker still has to test and repair the old harbour poles. Apprentices need paid time on a real span, not just a neat screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role seems steady, my partner's school kitchen shifts are regular, and we have four months of expenses set aside. Retirement is near enough to discuss, though I have not chosen a year or checked every number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep directing the harbour pole replacements and check each isolation with the crew. At the next worker safety meeting I'll ask the union branch to protect paid apprentice climbing hours in the yearly training plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our pay, with the usual care about a four-month reserve. The paperwork change itself would not make me lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a field check beat a photograph?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we stopped at an old harbour pole after a rough night. The harbour power-pole photograph looked sound until our apprentice saw the split crossarm from the bucket. We replaced the timber before moving the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your union branch actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch to put paid bucket practice in writing and take it to the company training meeting. I am already a member, but this is a proposal I would actually bring to a group.

say: **Harbour poles** still need physical tests and repair crews when office forms become shorter.
**Paid apprentice climbs** should remain in the training plan.
think: My **lead shifts** and my partner's kitchen work feel steady.
Our **four-month reserve** supports retirement planning without forcing a date today.
do: **Keep** directing harbour pole repairs and checking each isolation.
**Propose** paid apprentice bucket hours at the union safety meeting.
feel: **Calm** about income and the small paperwork change.
S0.quote: The harbour power-pole photograph looked sound until our apprentice saw the split crossarm from the bucket.
fieldNote: He prefers **physical inspection** and makes an actual union training proposal.
A four-month reserve and steady household wages support **calm** with no fixed retirement year.

steps.text: Keep directing harbour pole repairs and checking isolation
Propose paid apprentice bucket hours at union safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may book repairs and buy fittings, while robots take longer to handle a power pole. The company must give field crews time to question a generated isolation plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on role should remain, but fewer dispatchers could mean shorter paid callouts and more unpaid checking for me. Four months saved gives us a little room, not a reason to shrug at a wage cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a record of callout hours for the first six months after any new scheduler. At a union branch meeting I'll compare those hours with the prior season and ask for paid plan-checking time and a written stop-work rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a realistic reduction in paid hours, though I could still keep the lead job. A computer's speed cannot become my unpaid evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the generated isolation plan looks complete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold the crew at the depot gate, call control and verify which switch is open. A complete power-line plan can still send my crew to the wrong open switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would the branch bring to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring six months of wage slips, not just a complaint. If the hours have not changed, I'd still seek the stop rule because the safety risk is separate.

say: **Generated plans** need time for a crew to challenge their isolation points.
**Paid checking** should replace work shifted from a smaller dispatch office.
think: My **callout hours** could shrink even while the repair post remains.
A **four-month cushion** helps briefly but cannot make a continuing wage cut harmless.
do: **Record** six months of callout pay after any AI scheduler starts.
**Bring** wage slips to union meeting for paid checks and stop-work rule.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss and unpaid checking.
S1.quote: A complete power-line plan can still send my crew to the wrong open switch.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **wage evidence** in the recorded callout hours from a separate written stop-work safety request.
Possible reduced **paid callouts** justify anxiety despite high standing.

steps.text: Record six months of callout pay if AI scheduler starts
Bring wage slips and stop-work request to union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI by 2028 will hit dispatch first, with capable pole-repair robots around 2031. I want a written count of the crews that will still be paid to climb and test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 when robots reach the field, and I may still need the line wage. The company may decide an older lead is too expensive. Four months of savings cannot carry a power-line worker through years of missing shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the union branch for a meeting with management on 2028 dispatch and 2031 line staffing. My partner and I will compare retirement income against household bills, and I'll check nearby utilities for actual paid crew openings before any job move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of shifts, with some local options and time to ask questions. I do not know a cut is certain, so I won't tell the family it has happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown son we are getting the figures and keeping our normal bills paid. He has his own household, and I don't plan to make him a bridge to retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply to another utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for advance notice and paid transfer places if the company trims crews. I would apply to another utility only after a real hours cut or a better paid vacancy, not because a machine appeared in a demonstration.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before 2031 field robots threaten pole shifts.
The company should publish **paid crew counts** and transfer terms.
think: At about **63**, I may still need wages when robots enter field repair.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot bridge a long cut before affordable retirement.
do: **Join** union meeting with management on 2028 and 2031 staffing.
**Compare** retirement income with bills before changing exit plans.
**Check** nearby utilities for paid crew openings before any job move.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour loss, with union and local job options.
S2.quote: Four months of savings cannot carry a power-line worker through years of missing shifts.
fieldNote: He treats retirement cost checks as **information**, not an early-exit decision.
The job search is **conditional** on actual cuts or a better paid opening.
His union demand has **specific dates** for dispatch and field staffing.

steps.text: Join union meeting on 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing
Compare retirement income against household bills
Check nearby utility vacancies before any job move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to thinking AI in 2031 gives the company time to plan for robots around 2034. A safe transition should include paid ground inspection work for people who know the old lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66, I might want ground checks rather than bucket climbs if our retirement sums are still short. No inspection post is promised, and the household budget may still depend on my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union branch to put full-wage ground inspection posts on its bargaining agenda. Starting next pay, we'll put the cancelled streaming subscription cost toward the mortgage while both incomes hold; I'll apply for a ground post if one is actually funded and its pay covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage gap, even with more time. I can use that time to ask for funded posts. I want the plan written as hours and pay, not as a kind word about experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What duties would make an inspection post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how many days an inspector walks the route and who signs the test. A training-yard visit is not the full power-line inspection wage our household might still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra mortgage payment come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra mortgage payment is the cost of a subscription we will cancel, sent from each new pay packet. If my partner's kitchen hours fall, we'd keep the normal payment instead.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes planning ahead of field robots around 2034.
**Ground inspection posts** should have full wages and real testing duties.
think: At about **66**, lighter work might fit if retirement still needs my wage.
No **inspection vacancy** exists yet, so I cannot assume a safe transition.
do: **Put** full-wage ground inspection jobs on union bargaining agenda.
**Overpay** mortgage from cancelled subscription cost while both incomes hold.
**Apply** for funded ground inspection post if pay covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour loss before retirement is affordable.
S3.quote: A training-yard visit is not the full power-line inspection wage our household might still need.
fieldNote: He seeks **funded duties** and adequate pay before considering a move.
The mortgage plan is **new debt payment** from wages, conditional on both household incomes.

steps.text: Put full-wage ground jobs on union bargaining agenda
Overpay mortgage from cancelled subscription while both incomes hold
Apply for funded ground inspection post if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 would reach dispatch first, and field robots around 2039 come when I would be about 71. By then I hope retirement is affordable, and I want the apprentice training plan left in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long timeline is less threatening to my own wage, but our four months saved do not settle a retirement date. I will not promise to stop work until income covers the ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will review our retirement statements and the mortgage balance. I'll keep directing line repairs while I can, and bring the apprentice-hours proposal to the branch until a younger member agrees to carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the household sums, calmer about robots. A decade is time to prepare, not a payment into the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before leaving the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a younger worker the old switch that is easy to misread at night. My technical diploma matters only if another lineworker can test the old feeder after I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a union handover include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the branch a written list of paid bucket hours and the person who checks each trainee. I want someone to present it at the next company meeting, not store it in a drawer.

say: **2036 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before 2039 field robots reach repairs.
**Paid apprentice hours** still need a named union advocate when I leave.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be retired if the household figures work.
Our **four-month reserve** alone cannot fix a final work date.
do: **Review** retirement statements and mortgage balance with partner this year.
**Keep** directing repairs while safe and needed.
**Hand** paid apprentice-hour proposal to younger union member at branch meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement sums, relatively calm about the later robot date.
S4.quote: My technical diploma matters only if another lineworker can test the old feeder after I leave.
fieldNote: He treats 2039 as **beyond hoped-for work**, contingent on retirement affordability.
The branch handover is a **specific proposal** with paid hours and a named presenter.

steps.text: Review retirement statements and mortgage balance with partner
Keep directing line repairs while safe and needed
Hand apprentice-hours proposal to younger union member at branch meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots around 2031 could cut my line shifts when I am about 63 and may still need wages. Written crew counts and funded ground inspection posts would let us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to teach the next person the old harbour switches. A line crew can have a perfect plan on a screen and still climb the wrong power pole. I want the check and the teaching written into the job, not offered as a favour.

headlineQuote: A line crew can have a perfect plan on a screen and still climb the wrong power pole.
portrait: **Marco**, 58, leads harbour line repairs using a two-year technical diploma and long knowledge of old feeders.
He has **never used AI** and pursues paid safety checks and apprentice practice through a union branch.
His **typical pay**, school-kitchen partner and four-month reserve make retirement planning necessary while some local crews offer alternatives.
Fast field robots make him **anxious** about a wage gap; a longer runway lets him seek funded ground work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots around 2031 before his retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: Written **crew counts** and funded ground inspection posts would help him plan.
